claims.source: Expressing qui-1 selectively in ADL rescues both the qui-1 ADL neurosecretory phenotype and enhanced escape from 21% O2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figures 2B and 3A.

claims.claim: Profiling ADL neurons in qui-1 mutants highlights extensive changes in gene expression, notably of many neuropeptide receptors.
claims.source: Profiling ADL neurons in qui-1 mutants highlights extensive changes in gene expression, notably of many neuropeptide receptors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5 and supplementary files.

claims.claim: Elevated ADL expression of the conserved neuropeptide receptor NPR-22 is necessary for enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: We show that elevated ADL expression of the conserved neuropeptide receptor NPR-22 is necessary for enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants, and is sufficient to confer increased ADL neurosecretion in control animals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments showing that npr-22 deletion reduces neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: Elevated ADL expression of NPR-22 is sufficient to confer increased ADL neurosecretion in control animals.
claims.source: We show that elevated ADL expression of the conserved neuropeptide receptor NPR-22 is necessary for enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants, and is sufficient to confer increased ADL neurosecretion in control animals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Sensory loss can confer cross-modal plasticity by changing the peptidergic connectome.
claims.source: Sensory loss can thus confer cross-modal plasticity by changing the peptidergic connectome.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is supported by inference from the results.

claims.claim: In blind people the absence of visual stimulation leads to rewiring of inputs into primary visual cortex (V1), so that V1 becomes responsive to tactile stimuli.
claims.source: For example, in blind people the absence of visual stimulation leads to rewiring of inputs into primary visual cortex (V1), so that V1 becomes responsive to tactile stimuli, a characteristic absent in sighted individuals (Büchel et al., 1998; Dietrich et al., 2013; Sadato et al., 1996; Wanet-Defalque et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in humans.

claims.claim: Animals acclimated to 21% O2 are attracted to pheromones that repel animals acclimated to 7% O2.
claims.source: For example, animals acclimated to 21% O2 are attracted to pheromones that repel animals acclimated to 7% O2 (Fenk and de Bono, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: URX O2 sensors show persistent higher activity at 21% O2 compared to 7% O2.
claims.source: The URX O2 sensors show persistent higher activity at 21% O2 compared to 7% O2, and tonically transmit this activity to the RMG hub interneurons (Busch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: URX tonically transmits activity to the RMG hub interneurons.
claims.source: The URX O2 sensors show persistent higher activity at 21% O2 compared to 7% O2, and tonically transmit this activity to the RMG hub interneurons (Busch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: NPR-1 215V inhibits O2-escape behaviour by acting in the RMG interneurons to reduce the output of the hub-and-spoke circuit.
claims.source: NPR-1 215V inhibits O2-escape behaviour by acting in the RMG interneurons to reduce the output of the hub-and-spoke circuit (Macosko et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: qui-1(db104) mutants display both aggregation and O2-escape behaviour.
claims.source: qui-1(db104) mutants isolated in our screen displayed both aggregation and O2-escape behaviour (Figure 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: qui-1(db104) and qui-1(ok3571) strains showed indistinguishable O2-escape responses.
claims.source: We next compared the O2-escape behaviour of the db104 mutant with a strain carrying a deletion allele, qui-1(ok3571) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). These strains showed indistinguishable responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), further suggesting that disrupting qui-1 confers strong O2-escape behaviour.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing two different qui-1 alleles shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: A wild-type qui-1 transgene completely rescued the qui-1(db104) O2-escape phenotype.
claims.source: To confirm this, we showed that a wild-type qui-1 transgene completely rescued the qui-1(db104) O2-escape phenotype (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: qui-1 Ca2+ responses in URX, AQR, PQR, and RMG neurons resembled those of wild-type controls.
claims.source: qui-1 Ca2+ responses in each of these neurons resembled those of wild-type controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), suggesting that the augmented O2-escape behaviour of qui-1 animals does not reflect a simple increase in the activity of O2 sensors or RMG interneurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claims.claim: The augmented O2-escape behaviour of qui-1 animals does not reflect a simple increase in the activity of O2 sensors or RMG interneurons.
claims.source: qui-1 Ca2+ responses in each of these neurons resembled those of wild-type controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), suggesting that the augmented O2-escape behaviour of qui-1 animals does not reflect a simple increase in the activity of O2 sensors or RMG interneurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging data showing no difference between qui-1 and controls.

claims.claim: QUI-1 is an ortholog of NWD1 (Nacht and WD40 repeat domain containing 1).
claims.source: Previous work (Hilliard et al., 2004) and homology searches suggest QUI-1 is an ortholog of NWD1 (Nacht and WD40 repeat domain containing 1), a conserved protein of poorly understood function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: mNeonGreen::QUI-1 fusion protein was confined to head and tail neurons, including ASH, ADL, PHB, and PVQ.
claims.source: Fluorescence from the mNeonGreen::QUI-1 fusion protein was confined to head and tail neurons, and we observed expression in ASH, ADL, PHB, and PVQ as previously reported (Figure 1E and Hilliard et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The mNeonGreen::QUI-1 fusion protein appears to be largely cytosolic and excluded from the nucleus.
claims.source: The mNeonGreen::QUI-1 fusion protein appears to be largely cytosolic and excluded from the nucleus, consistent with previous reports (Figure 1E and Neal et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1E and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Expressing qui-1 selectively in ASH neurons reduced the O2-escape response of qui-1 mutants compared to wild-type animals.
claims.source: Expressing qui-1 selectively in ASH neurons reduced the O2-escape response of qui-1 mutants compared to wild-type animals (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Expressing qui-1 only in ADL significantly reduced the O2-evoked escape behaviour of qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: Expressing qui-1 only in ADL also significantly reduced the O2-evoked escape behaviour of qui-1 mutants (Figure 2B), but as with targeted expression in ASH, rescue was incomplete and transgenic animals responded significantly more to a 21% O2 stimulus than wild-type animals (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Expressing QUI-1 in both ASH and ADL neurons did not show an additive rescue effect.
claims.source: Expressing QUI-1 in both ASH and ADL neurons did not show an additive rescue effect (Figure 2C), consistent with ablation studies suggesting these neurons act redundantly to promote aggregation behaviour (de Bono et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2C and inference from previous ablation studies.

claims.claim: QUI-1 acts in ASH, ADL, and potentially other neurons to downregulate O2-escape behaviour.
claims.source: We conclude that QUI-1 acts in ASH, ADL, and potentially other neurons to downregulate O2-escape behaviour.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the cell-specific rescue experiments.

claims.claim: qui-1 mutants lack pheromone-evoked Ca2+ responses in ADL.
claims.source: In wild-type control animals ADL neurons responded to the C9 ascaroside pheromone with a Ca2+ response, as expected (Jang et al., 2012), however this response was completely abolished in qui-1 mutants (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: QUI-1 is required for sensory transduction of pheromone stimuli.
claims.source: This suggests that QUI-1 is required for sensory transduction of pheromone stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the loss of pheromone-evoked Ca2+ responses in qui-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Loss of qui-1 abolished ADL O2-evoked Ca2+ responses.
claims.source: Surprisingly, loss of qui-1 abolished ADL O2-evoked Ca2+ responses, and stimulation with 21% O2 resulted, if anything, in a reduction of ADL's Ca2+ levels (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: A simple increase in O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in ADL does not explain the increased ability of qui-1 mutants to escape 21% O2.
claims.source: These data suggest that a simple increase in O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in ADL does not explain the increased ability of qui-1 mutants to escape 21% O2.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that qui-1 mutants show enhanced O2 escape but reduced Ca2+ responses in ADL.

claims.claim: There is a striking increase in ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants compared to control.
claims.source: Using this assay, we found a striking increase in ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants compared to control (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Expressing wild-type qui-1 exclusively in ADL fully rescued the enhanced neurosecretion phenotype.
claims.source: Expressing wild-type qui-1 exclusively in ADL fully rescued this enhanced neurosecretion phenotype (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Increased insulin secretion levels cannot be explained by increased expression from the srh-220 promoter.
claims.source: Increased insulin secretion levels cannot be explained by increased expression from the srh-220 promoter: the fluorescent intensity of free mKate expressed from this promoter was not altered in qui-1 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Disrupting QUI-1 function in ADL enhances neurosecretion from these neurons.
claims.source: These data suggest that disrupting QUI-1 function in ADL enhances neurosecretion from these neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the neurosecretion assays and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Loss of qui-1 does not lead to increased axonal accumulation of dense-core vesicles (DCVs).
claims.source: qui-1 mutants did not show gross differences in the axonal distribution of IDA-1::GFP (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data quantifying IDA-1::GFP in axons shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Enhanced neurosecretion from ADL in qui-1 mutants is not due to increased DCVs accumulation in axons but may reflect an increased rate of release.
claims.source: These data suggest that enhanced neurosecretion from ADL in qui-1 mutants is not due to increased DCVs accumulation in axons but may reflect an increased rate of release.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the DCV trafficking experiments showing no change in DCV distribution.

claims.claim: Disrupting gcy-35 almost completely abolished the enhanced neurosecretion of qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: Consistent with this, disrupting gcy-35 almost completely abolished the enhanced neurosecretion of qui-1 mutants (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data in qui-1;gcy-35 double mutants shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Overexpressing wild-type GCY-35 in URX rescued the ADL neurosecretion phenotype of qui-1;gcy-35 double mutants, although not completely.
claims.source: Overexpressing wild-type GCY-35 in URX, using the flp-8 or gcy-32 promoters, rescued the ADL neurosecretion phenotype of qui-1;gcy-35 double mutants, although not completely (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Increased neurosecretion from ADL neurons in qui-1 mutants reflects an enhanced response to O2 partly mediated by URX neurons.
claims.source: We conclude that increased neurosecretion from ADL neurons in qui-1 mutants reflects an enhanced response to O2 partly mediated by URX neurons.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the genetic experiments with gcy-35 and URX-specific rescue.

claims.claim: In control animals ADL neurosecretion was unaffected by O2 experience.
claims.source: In control animals ADL neurosecretion was unaffected by O2 experience (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data at different O2 levels shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Neurosecretion from ADL was significantly modulated by O2 experience in qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: By contrast, neurosecretion from ADL was significantly modulated by O2 experience in qui-1 mutants (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data at different O2 levels shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Mutants kept at low O2 concentrations showed markedly less ADL neurosecretion than animals kept at 21% O2.
claims.source: Mutants kept at low O2 concentrations showed markedly less ADL neurosecretion than animals kept at 21% O2 (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Disrupting qui-1 confers O2-evoked neurosecretion on ADL neurons.
claims.source: Together, these data support the hypothesis that disrupting qui-1 confers O2-evoked neurosecretion on ADL neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the O2-dependent modulation of ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants.

claims.claim: qui-1;npr-1 double mutants showed higher levels of neurosecretion from ADL than qui-1 single mutants.
claims.source: We observed higher levels of neurosecretion from ADL in qui-1;npr-1 double mutants (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Expressing NPR-1 215V in RMG partially rescued the ADL phenotype of qui-1;npr-1 double mutants.
claims.source: Expressing NPR-1 215V in RMG partially rescued the ADL phenotype of qui-1;npr-1 double mutants (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: NPR-1 signalling in RMG neurons can suppress neurosecretion from ADL.
claims.source: We conclude that NPR-1 signalling in RMG neurons can suppress neurosecretion from ADL.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with NPR-1 expression in RMG.

claims.claim: Enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants is principally driven by increased ADL responsiveness to O2 input from the hub-and-spoke circuit.
claims.source: Taken together, these and previous data suggest enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants is principally driven by increased ADL responsiveness to O2 input from the hub-and-spoke circuit.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from multiple genetic and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: bbs genes encode components of a large protein complex involved in intraflagellar transport, the BBsome.
claims.source: A group of genes involved in sensory perception and associated with Bardet–Biedl syndrome, called bbs genes in C. elegans, has been proposed to reduce, by an unknown mechanism, neurosecretion (Lee et al., 2011). bbs genes encode components of a large protein complex involved in intraflagellar transport, the BBsome, which couples cargo vesicles to motor proteins for delivery to cilia.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and established knowledge about BBS genes.

claims.claim: bbs mutants exhibit sensory defects and show increased DCV release from ADL.
claims.source: bbs mutants exhibit sensory defects, and, like qui-1, show increased DCV release from ADL (Lee et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: bbs-7 mutants showed increased activity at 21% O2, behaving like qui-1.
claims.source: Of the five bbs mutants we studied, three, bbs-1, -2, and -7, responded to 7% O2 by slowing down significantly more than N2; one, bbs-7, also showed increased activity at 21% O2, behaving like qui-1 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: wrt-6 and fig-1 mutants show increased O2-evoked behaviours.
claims.source: A search of the sequencing data from our mutant collection revealed two mutant strains carrying missense mutations in genes previously associated with impaired sensory perception, wrt-6 (WaRThog, a hedgehog-related protein) and fig-1 (dye-Filling abnormal, expressed In Glia) (Bacaj et al., 2008; Hao et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: A wild-type copy of wrt-6 entirely rescued the O2-escape phenotype of db102 mutants.
claims.source: A wild-type copy of wrt-6 entirely rescued the O2-escape phenotype of db102 mutants, confirming that this phenotype reflect loss of wrt-6 function (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: All fig-1 mutants showed an increased O2-response characterized by reduced locomotory activity at 7% O2.
claims.source: All fig-1 mutants showed an increased O2-response characterized by reduced locomotory activity at 7% O2 (Figure 4C), suggesting that the absence of fig-1 leads to stronger O2-evoked responses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: wrt-6 and fig-1 mutants showed a robust increase in ADL neurosecretion.
claims.source: To test this, we measured ADL neurosecretion in wrt-6 and fig-1 mutants and observed a robust increase in both mutants (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: bbs-7 mutants grown at 7% O2 lost their enhanced neurosecretion phenotype and showed secretion levels indistinguishable from control animals reared at 7% O2.
claims.source: bbs-7 mutants grown at 7% O2, when URX–RMG activity is low, lost their enhanced neurosecretion phenotype and showed secretion levels indistinguishable from control animals reared at 7% O2 (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data at different O2 levels shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: For bbs-7 and qui-1, enhanced ADL neurosecretion reflects increased responsiveness to O2 input.
claims.source: These data suggest that ADL neurons release more DCVs in bbs, wrt-6, and fig-1 mutants than controls. For bbs-7 and qui-1, and potentially for other sensory-defective mutants, enhanced ADL neurosecretion reflects increased responsiveness to O2 input.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the O2-dependent modulation of ADL neurosecretion in these mutants.

claims.claim: osm-6::AID knock-in animals did not show any defect compared to wild-type in their ability to take up DiO.
claims.source: osm-6::AID knock-in animals did not show any defect compared to wild-type in their ability to take up DiO (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B), suggesting that OSM-6::AID is functional.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye filling assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: ADL-restricted expression of TIR1 was sufficient to reduce ADL dye filling in osm-6::AID animals.
claims.source: ADL-restricted expression of the F-box protein TIR1, which selectively targets proteins containing the AID tag for degradation (Nishimura et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2015), was sufficient to reduce ADL dye filling in osm-6::AID animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C III and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye filling assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: Adding Auxin further reduced ADL dye filling compared to a control strain expressing TIR1 in ADL in the absence of the osm-6::AID allele.
claims.source: Adding Auxin further reduced ADL dye filling (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C IV and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D) compared to a control strain expressing TIR1 in ADL in the absence of the osm-6::AID allele.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye filling assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: osm-6::AID animals expressing TIR1 in ADL displayed elevated neurosecretion levels compared to osm-6::AID controls.
claims.source: osm-6::AID animals expressing TIR1 in ADL displayed elevated neurosecretion levels compared to osm-6::AID controls (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), whereas growing these animals in the presence of Auxin suppressed this increase (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Growing osm-6::AID animals expressing TIR1 in ADL in the presence of Auxin suppressed the increase in neurosecretion.
claims.source: osm-6::AID animals expressing TIR1 in ADL displayed elevated neurosecretion levels compared to osm-6::AID controls (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), whereas growing these animals in the presence of Auxin suppressed this increase (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Altering O2 concentrations modulated ADL neurosecretion levels only in osm-6::AID animals expressing TIR1 grown in the absence of Auxin.
claims.source: Altering O2 concentrations modulated ADL neurosecretion levels only in osm-6::AID animals expressing TIR1 grown in the absence of Auxin (Figure 4G), suggesting that limited impairment of OSM-6::AID in ADL confers O2-evoked neurosecretion on this neuron pair.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data at different O2 levels shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Limited impairing of OSM-6 function in ADL confers O2-evoked neurosecretion.
claims.source: We conclude that limited impairing of OSM-6 function in ADL confers O2-evoked neurosecretion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the OSM-6 knockdown experiments showing O2-dependent neurosecretion.

claims.claim: The enhanced coupling of ADL to the hub-and-spoke circuit observed in qui-1 and other sensory defective mutants most likely results from cell autonomous sensory defects in ADL.
claims.source: Taken together these data confirm that the enhanced coupling of ADL to the hub-and-spoke circuit observed in qui-1 and other sensory defective mutants most likely results from cell autonomous sensory defects in ADL.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the cell-specific OSM-6 knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Enrichment analysis highlighted ADL as the most enriched neural class in the RNAseq dataset.
claims.source: Enrichment analysis highlighted ADL as the most enriched neural class in our dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis of the RNAseq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: ADL expresses a large number of chemoreceptors.
claims.source: Consistent with its function as a chemosensory neuron, ADL expresses a large number of chemoreceptors (Supplementary file 2), as well as several neuropeptide receptors (Supplementary file 3) and neuropeptides (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data presented in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Principal component analysis confirmed that qui-1 samples could be robustly differentiated from control samples.
claims.source: Principal component analysis confirmed that we could robustly differentiate qui-1 from control samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The majority of differentially regulated genes were strongly upregulated in qui-1 mutant samples.
claims.source: The majority of differentially regulated genes were strongly upregulated in mutant samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claims.claim: Almost all known genes associated with DCV release that were differentially regulated showed elevated expression in qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: When we selected all known genes associated with DCV release (Hobert, 2013) that were also differentially regulated, almost all showed elevated expression in qui-1 mutants (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: More than half of all the chemoreceptors expressed in ADL were differentially regulated in qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: qui-1 mutants also showed altered chemosensory receptor levels: more than half of all the chemoreceptors expressed in ADL were differentially regulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F.

claims.claim: Loss of qui-1 extensively remodels ADL gene expression.
claims.source: These data suggest that loss of qui-1 extensively remodels ADL gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the extensive changes in gene expression observed in the RNAseq data.

claims.claim: Several neuropeptide receptors were differentially expressed in ADL between control and qui-1.
claims.source: Several neuropeptide receptors were differentially expressed in ADL between control and qui-1 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: npr-22 was one of the most highly upregulated genes in qui-1 mutants compared to control.
claims.source: Most prominent of these was neuropeptide receptor 22 (npr-22), which was one of the most highly upregulated genes in qui-1 mutants compared to control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: qui-1;npr-22 double mutants showed significantly reduced neurosecretion compared to qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: The double mutant showed significantly reduced neurosecretion compared to qui-1 mutants (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Selectively expressing npr-22 in ADL completely rescued the neurosecretion phenotype of qui-1;npr-22 double mutants.
claims.source: This phenotype was completely rescued by selectively expressing npr-22 in ADL, confirming that npr-22 is necessary to sustain ADL's higher neurosecretion levels in qui-1 mutants, and acts in ADL itself.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: npr-22 is necessary to sustain ADL's higher neurosecretion levels in qui-1 mutants and acts in ADL itself.
claims.source: This phenotype was completely rescued by selectively expressing npr-22 in ADL, confirming that npr-22 is necessary to sustain ADL's higher neurosecretion levels in qui-1 mutants, and acts in ADL itself.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Increasing npr-22 expression was sufficient to induce a higher rate of neurosecretion from ADL.
claims.source: To test if inducing npr-22 expression is sufficient to stimulate ADL neurosecretion, we overexpressed the neuropeptide receptor in wild-type ADL neurons. Increasing npr-22 expression was sufficient to induce a higher rate of neurosecretion from ADL (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Increased peptidergic signalling through NPR-22 is necessary and sufficient to promote ADL neurosecretion.
claims.source: These data suggest increased peptidergic signalling through NPR-22 is necessary and sufficient to promote ADL neurosecretion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the loss-of-function and overexpression experiments with npr-22.

claims.claim: Loss of tkr-1 significantly decreased neurosecretion from ADL to levels comparable to those in qui-1;npr-22.
claims.source: The second such neuropeptide receptor gene in our list (Figure 5B) was the TachyKinin Receptor 1, tkr-1. Loss of tkr-1 also significantly decreased neurosecretion from ADL to levels comparable to those in qui-1;npr-22 (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neurosecretion assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Both qui-1;npr-22 and qui-1;tkr-1 animals show O2-escape responses similar to those of qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: Both qui-1;npr-22 and qui-1;tkr-1 animals show O2-escape responses similar to those of qui-1 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B), and overexpressing npr-22 in ADL neurons did not confer increased O2-escape behaviour compared to wild-type animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: Overexpressing npr-22 in ADL neurons did not confer increased O2-escape behaviour compared to wild-type animals.
claims.source: Both qui-1;npr-22 and qui-1;tkr-1 animals show O2-escape responses similar to those of qui-1 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B), and overexpressing npr-22 in ADL neurons did not confer increased O2-escape behaviour compared to wild-type animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: While increased expression of npr-22 and tkr-1 underpin increased ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants, they are not sufficient to explain the increased O2-escape behaviour in these animals.
claims.source: This suggests that while increased expression of npr-22 and tkr-1 underpin increased ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants, they are not sufficient to explain the increased O2-escape behaviour in these animals.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral and neurosecretion data.

claims.claim: The O2-escape behaviour of qui-1 animals expressing TeTX in ADL was similar to that of qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: The O2-escape behaviour of qui-1 animals expressing TeTX in ADL was similar to that of qui-1 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that ADL neurosecretion is not essential for the increased O2-escape response of qui-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: ADL neurosecretion is not essential for the increased O2-escape response of qui-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Disrupting sensory responsiveness in ADL increases the coupling of this neuron to the hub-and-spoke circuit by reconfiguring the expression of neuropeptide receptors that facilitate DCVs release.
claims.source: We conclude that disrupting sensory responsiveness in ADL, by the qui-1 mutation, increases the coupling of this neuron to the hub-and-spoke circuit by reconfiguring the expression of neuropeptide receptors that facilitate DCVs release.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data.

claims.claim: Loss of QUI-1 prevents the ADL sensory neurons from responding to pheromone.
claims.source: We show that loss of QUI-1 prevents the ADL sensory neurons from responding to pheromone, but increases ADL neurosecretion in response to input from upstream O2-sensing neurons.

claims.claim: Loss of QUI-1 increases ADL neurosecretion in response to input from upstream O2-sensing neurons.
claims.source: We show that loss of QUI-1 prevents the ADL sensory neurons from responding to pheromone, but increases ADL neurosecretion in response to input from upstream O2-sensing neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by neurosecretion assay data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Loss of qui-1 recruits ADL sensory neurons more strongly into the O2-sensing circuit.
claims.source: Loss of qui-1 thus recruits ADL sensory neurons more strongly into the O2-sensing circuit.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced O2-evoked neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Loss of qui-1 is associated with extensive changes in gene expression in ADL neurons, notably induced expression of neuropeptide receptors, including NPR-22 and TKR-1.
claims.source: Loss of qui-1 is associated with extensive changes in gene expression in ADL neurons, notably induced expression of neuropeptide receptors, including NPR-22 and TKR-1.

claims.claim: Elevated expression of NPR-22 and TKR-1 increase the coupling of ADL neurosecretion to O2 input in qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: Elevated expression of NPR-22 and TKR-1 increase the coupling of ADL neurosecretion to O2 input in qui-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments showing that npr-22 and tkr-1 are necessary for enhanced neurosecretion.

claims.claim: Impairing sensory perception can sensitize sensory neurons to other sensory modalities by reconfiguring peptidergic circuits.
claims.source: We propose that impairing sensory perception can sensitize sensory neurons to other sensory modalities by reconfiguring peptidergic circuits.
claims.evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: ADL-specific expression of qui-1 rescues both the increased O2-escape phenotype of qui-1 mutants and enhanced neurosecretion from ADL, indicating that qui-1 acts cell autonomously to regulate neurosecretion.
claims.source: ADL-specific expression of qui-1 rescues both the increased O2-escape phenotype of qui-1 mutants and enhanced neurosecretion from ADL (Figures 2B and 3A), indicating that qui-1 acts cell autonomously to regulate neurosecretion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cell-specific rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Impairing the primary O2-sensing mechanism by disrupting GCY-35 restores ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants to levels observed in controls.
claims.source: Impairing the primary O2-sensing mechanism, by disrupting the molecular oxygen sensor GCY-35, restores ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants to levels observed in controls (Figure 3C), confirming that increased ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 is driven primarily by activity originating outside ADL.
claims.evidence: This is supported by neurosecretion assay data in qui-1;gcy-35 double mutants.

claims.claim: Increased ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 is driven primarily by activity originating outside ADL.
claims.source: Impairing the primary O2-sensing mechanism, by disrupting the molecular oxygen sensor GCY-35, restores ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants to levels observed in controls (Figure 3C), confirming that increased ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 is driven primarily by activity originating outside ADL.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the gcy-35 experiments.

claims.claim: In qui-1 mutants ADL neurons are more sensitive to incoming pre-synaptic activity.
claims.source: Together with data showing that qui-1 mutants exhibit normal O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in the primary O2-sensing neurons URX, AQR, PQR, and in the hub interneurons RMG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), this suggests that in qui-1 mutants ADL neurons are more sensitive to incoming pre-synaptic activity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of normal upstream Ca2+ responses and enhanced ADL neurosecretion.

claims.claim: URX helps drive increased ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: Selectively expressing gcy-35 cDNA in the URX O2 sensors partially rescues the ADL neurosecretion phenotype of qui-1;gcy-35 mutants (Figure 3D), confirming that URX helps drive increased ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Activity from the hub-and-spoke circuit propagates from URX–RMG to ADL to stimulate neurosecretion.
claims.source: Disrupting the inhibitory neuropeptide receptor npr-1 further increases ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants, and this phenotype is partially rescued by expressing npr-1 cDNA specifically in RMG interneurons (Figure 3F). This further supports a model in which activity from the hub-and-spoke circuit propagates from URX–RMG to ADL to stimulate neurosecretion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic experiments with npr-1.

claims.claim: Disrupting qui-1 recruits ADL more strongly into the hub-and-spoke circuit.
claims.source: Consistent with this, in qui-1 mutants, but not in controls, ADL neurons show O2-evoked neurosecretion: prolonged exposure to low (7%) or high (21%) O2 concentrations modulates ADL neurosecretion (Figure 3E). These data confirm that disrupting qui-1 recruits ADL more strongly into the hub-and-spoke circuit.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the O2-dependent modulation of ADL neurosecretion.

claims.claim: Blocking ADL's output by expressing TeTX has no effect on the O2-escape behaviour of qui-1 mutants.
claims.source: Blocking ADL's output by expressing TeTX has no effect on the O2-escape behaviour of qui-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Mutations in bbs-7 cause defects in cilia formation and in sensory perception.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that mutations in BBS-7, a conserved protein involved in trafficking of molecular cargos along the primary cilium of neurons, and linked to Bardet–Biedl syndrome (Liu and Lechtreck, 2018; Tan et al., 2007), lead to increased neurosecretion from ADL (Lee et al., 2011). Mutations in bbs-7 cause defects in cilia formation and in sensory perception.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Increased neurosecretion from ADL in bbs mutants may reflect increased coupling to the O2 circuit.
claims.source: Our data suggest that increased neurosecretion from ADL in bbs mutants may reflect increased coupling to the O2 circuit (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the O2-dependent neurosecretion in bbs-7 mutants.

claims.claim: bbs-7 mutants show a range of other physiological phenotypes including small body size and delays in development.
claims.source: Interestingly, bbs-7 mutants show a range of other physiological phenotypes including small body size and delays in development (Lee et al., 2011; Mok et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Both small body size and developmental delays in bbs-7 mutants can be suppressed by mutating gcy-35.
claims.source: Both of these phenotypes can be suppressed by mutating gcy-35 (Mok et al., 2011), consistent with them resulting from enhanced responses to O2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Cell-specific sensory defects in ADL result in heightened responsiveness to O2 inputs which support an increased ADL neurosecretion.
claims.source: Cell-specific sensory defects in ADL result in heightened responsiveness to O2 inputs which support an increased ADL neurosecretion (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the OSM-6 knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: While mildly disrupting ADL's cilium function increases ADL responsiveness to O2 inputs, a greater impairment does not result in the same alteration.

The TIR1 system used in this study makes it difficult to assess OSM-6::AID levels in the absence or presence of Auxin, however we speculate that while mildly disrupting ADL's cilium function increases ADL responsiveness to O2 inputs, a greater impairment does not result in the same alteration.
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the Auxin experiments.

claims.claim: Both fig-1 and wrt-6 display increased ADL neurosecretion and an enhanced O2 response, despite both genes being expressed in glial cells.
claims.source: This is further supported by the fact that both fig-1 and wrt-6 display increased ADL neurosecretion and an enhanced O2 response, despite both genes being expressed in glial cells, suggesting their effect on ADL is indirect.
claims.evidence: This is supported by neurosecretion and behavioral data for these mutants.

claims.claim: Glia are required for proper cilia development and correct sensory perception.
claims.source: Glia are required for proper cilia development and correct sensory perception, and both glia-ablated animals and fig-1 mutants show defective responses to cues sensed by ADL (Bacaj et al., 2008).

claims.claim: wrt-6 mutants exhibit a dye filling defect.
claims.source: wrt-6 mutants also exhibit a dye filling defect (data not shown), suggesting impairment in ADL's ability to sense external cues.

claims.claim: The enhanced responsiveness to O2 input observed in sensory defective mutants is consistent with cell-specific defects in ADL sensory perception.
claims.source: These data taken together suggest that the enhanced responsiveness to O2 input we observe in sensory defective mutants, characterized by increased O2-evoked neurosecretion from ADL, is consistent with cell-specific defects in ADL sensory perception.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the collective data on sensory defective mutants.

claims.claim: Loss of a sensory modality can lead to recruitment of input-deprived sensory cortex to process information from spared senses.
claims.source: Conceptually, our findings resonate with studies in vertebrates which find that loss of a sensory modality can lead to recruitment of input-deprived sensory cortex to process information from spared senses (Lee and Whitt, 2015; Petrus et al., 2014; Rauschecker, 1995).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in vertebrates.

claims.claim: In the nervous system of C. elegans, the defective ADL sensory neurons become sensitized to pre-synaptic input associated with a different modality, O2 sensing.
claims.source: In the nervous system of C. elegans, the defective ADL sensory neurons becomes sensitized to pre-synaptic input associated with a different modality, O2 sensing (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claims.claim: This recruitment is supported by a transcriptional program in the sensory defective ADL that induces the expression of neuropeptide receptors including NPR-22 and TKR-1.
claims.source: This recruitment is supported by a transcriptional program in the sensory defective ADL that induces the expression of neuropeptide receptors including NPR-22 and TKR-1 (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Reconfigured peptidergic circuits may be a common feature of cross-modal recruitment.
claims.source: We speculate that reconfigured peptidergic circuits may be a common feature of cross-modal recruitment.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

results.result: A forward genetic screen identified qui-1 mutants that exhibit both enhanced O2-escape behavior and aggregation on thick food. The qui-1(db104) allele was confirmed by comparison with a deletion allele qui-1(ok3571) and rescue with wild-type qui-1 transgene.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C18, C19, and C20 provide converging evidence from behavioral assays, allelic comparison, and genetic rescue experiments that qui-1 mutants display enhanced O2 responses. The use of two independent alleles and successful rescue strongly support the genetic basis of the phenotype.

results.result: qui-1 mutants show normal Ca2+ responses in O2-sensing neurons (URX, AQR, PQR) and RMG interneurons, indicating that enhanced O2-escape behavior does not result from increased activity in these upstream neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C22 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F) showing no difference in O2-evoked Ca2+ responses between qui-1 and controls in key circuit neurons. This rules out a simple gain-of-function mechanism in upstream O2 sensors.

results.result: QUI-1 is a conserved NACHT/WD40 protein orthologous to mammalian NWD1, expressed in specific head and tail neurons including ASH, ADL, PHB, and PVQ, with cytosolic localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C23, C24, and C25 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), fluorescence microscopy of mNeonGreen::QUI-1 fusion protein (Figure 1E), and citations to previous work. The molecular characterization is well-documented.

results.result: Cell-specific rescue experiments demonstrate that QUI-1 acts in ASH and ADL neurons to downregulate O2-escape behavior, with these neurons acting redundantly.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C27, C28, and C29 are supported by cell-specific rescue data (Figures 2A, 2B, 2C) showing partial rescue when qui-1 is expressed in ASH or ADL individually, with no additive effect when expressed in both. This is consistent with redundant function.

results.result: qui-1 mutants completely lack pheromone-evoked Ca2+ responses in ADL neurons, indicating QUI-1 is required for sensory transduction of pheromone stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C31, and C5 are directly supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 2D) showing abolished pheromone responses in qui-1 mutants. The complete loss of response provides strong evidence for QUI-1's role in pheromone sensing.

results.result: Loss of qui-1 abolishes O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in ADL, indicating that enhanced O2-escape behavior in qui-1 mutants is not explained by increased Ca2+ responses in ADL.
results.evaluation: Claims C32 and C33 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 2E) showing reduced or abolished O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in qui-1 ADL neurons. This paradoxical finding is important for understanding the mechanism of enhanced O2 responses.

results.result: qui-1 mutants show dramatically increased neurosecretion from ADL neurons despite abolished Ca2+ responses. This enhanced neurosecretion is rescued by ADL-specific expression of qui-1 and is not due to increased promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C35, C36, C37, C6, and C7 are supported by neurosecretion assays (Figure 3A) and control experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The cell-specific rescue confirms qui-1 acts autonomously in ADL. The dissociation between Ca2+ and neurosecretion is a key finding.

results.result: Enhanced neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants is not due to increased accumulation of dense-core vesicles (DCVs) in axons, suggesting an increased rate of release rather than altered trafficking.
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C39 are supported by IDA-1::GFP imaging data (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C) showing no difference in DCV distribution between qui-1 and controls. This helps narrow down the mechanism to release regulation.

results.result: Enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants depends on the O2 sensor GCY-35 and is partly mediated by URX neurons, indicating increased ADL responsiveness to O2 input from upstream neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C41, C42, C96, C97, and C99 are supported by genetic epistasis experiments (Figure 3C, 3D) showing that gcy-35 mutation suppresses qui-1 neurosecretion phenotype and URX-specific rescue partially restores it. This establishes the circuit logic.

results.result: ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants is modulated by O2 experience (7% vs 21% O2), while control animals show no such modulation, confirming that qui-1 loss confers O2-evoked neurosecretion on ADL.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, C45, C46, and C101 are supported by neurosecretion assays at different O2 levels (Figure 3E). The O2-dependent modulation in qui-1 but not controls provides strong evidence for altered circuit coupling.

results.result: NPR-1 signaling in RMG neurons suppresses ADL neurosecretion, as shown by increased neurosecretion in qui-1;npr-1 double mutants and partial rescue by RMG-specific NPR-1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C48, C49, and C100 are supported by genetic experiments (Figure 3F) showing epistatic interactions between qui-1 and npr-1, with cell-specific rescue confirming RMG as the site of action. This establishes the circuit pathway from URX-RMG to ADL.

results.result: Multiple sensory-defective mutants (bbs-7, wrt-6, fig-1) show increased O2-evoked behaviors and enhanced ADL neurosecretion, suggesting a general principle linking sensory defects to enhanced O2 responsiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C54, C55, C56, and C57 are supported by behavioral and neurosecretion assays (Figures 4A, 4B, 4C, 4D) across multiple independent mutants. The convergence of phenotypes across different genes strengthens the generality of the finding.

results.result: Enhanced ADL neurosecretion in bbs-7 mutants is O2-dependent, being lost when animals are grown at 7% O2, indicating increased responsiveness to O2 input rather than constitutive activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C59, and C104 are supported by neurosecretion assays at different O2 levels (Figure 4E). The O2-dependence of the phenotype in bbs-7 parallels the qui-1 results and supports the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Cell-specific knockdown of OSM-6 in ADL using the AID system confers O2-evoked neurosecretion, demonstrating that cell-autonomous sensory defects in ADL are sufficient to enhance coupling to the O2 circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 and C107 are supported by dye-filling assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and neurosecretion assays (Figures 4F, 4G) using the OSM-6::AID system. The cell-specific manipulation provides strong evidence for cell autonomy, though the Auxin-independent effect of TIR1 noted in C108 adds some complexity.

results.result: RNA-seq profiling of ADL neurons in qui-1 mutants reveals extensive transcriptional remodeling, including upregulation of genes involved in DCV release, altered chemoreceptor expression, and differential expression of neuropeptide receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 and C9 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files). The enrichment analysis, PCA, and differential expression analysis are appropriate. However, the authors acknowledge potential contribution from background mutations despite outcrossing.

results.result: The neuropeptide receptor NPR-22 is highly upregulated in qui-1 ADL neurons and is necessary for enhanced neurosecretion, as shown by suppression in qui-1;npr-22 double mutants and rescue by ADL-specific npr-22 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 and C10 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and genetic experiments (Figure 5C). The loss-of-function and rescue experiments provide strong evidence for NPR-22's necessity.

results.result: Overexpression of NPR-22 in wild-type ADL neurons is sufficient to increase neurosecretion, demonstrating that elevated NPR-22 alone can drive enhanced neurosecretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C81, and C11 are supported by overexpression experiments (Figure 5D). The sufficiency experiment complements the necessity data and strongly supports NPR-22's role in promoting neurosecretion.

results.result: The tachykinin receptor TKR-1 also contributes to enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants, with loss of tkr-1 reducing neurosecretion to levels comparable to qui-1;npr-22.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is supported by neurosecretion assays in qui-1;tkr-1 mutants (Figure 5E). The similar magnitude of suppression by npr-22 and tkr-1 mutations suggests both receptors contribute substantially.

results.result: While NPR-22 and TKR-1 are necessary for enhanced ADL neurosecretion, they are not sufficient to explain increased O2-escape behavior in qui-1 mutants, and ADL neurosecretion itself is not essential for the behavioral phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 and C102 are supported by behavioral assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D) showing that disrupting npr-22, tkr-1, or blocking ADL neurosecretion with TeTX does not suppress qui-1 O2-escape behavior. This dissociation between neurosecretion and behavior is important but leaves the behavioral mechanism unclear.

results.result: The authors propose that impairing sensory perception in ADL increases its coupling to the O2-sensing circuit through transcriptional reconfiguration of neuropeptide receptor expression, representing a mechanism for cross-modal plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C91, C94, C114, C115, and C12 represent the main conclusions synthesized from all experimental data. The model is well-supported by the convergence of genetic, imaging, transcriptomic, and functional evidence, though some mechanistic details remain unclear (e.g., how sensory defects trigger transcriptional changes, how enhanced neurosecretion relates to behavior).

results.result: qui-1 acts cell-autonomously in ADL to regulate neurosecretion and O2-escape behavior, with qui-1 mutant ADL neurons showing increased sensitivity to presynaptic input despite normal upstream Ca2+ responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C98, and C8 are supported by cell-specific rescue experiments (Figures 2B, 3A) and the combination of normal upstream Ca2+ responses with enhanced ADL neurosecretion. The inference of increased sensitivity is logical given the data.

results.result: Enhanced ADL neurosecretion in qui-1 mutants is principally driven by increased ADL responsiveness to O2 input from the hub-and-spoke circuit, particularly from URX-RMG.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C42 synthesize multiple lines of evidence including gcy-35 epistasis, URX rescue, npr-1 interactions, and O2-dependent modulation. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective data.

results.result: The authors speculate that mild disruption of ADL cilium function increases O2 responsiveness, while greater impairment does not, based on Auxin-dependent suppression of the OSM-6 knockdown phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is explicitly labeled as speculation by the authors. The Auxin-dependent suppression (Figure 4F, 4G) is observed, but the authors acknowledge difficulty in assessing OSM-6::AID levels, making the dose-response interpretation uncertain. This non-monotonic relationship requires further investigation.

results.result: fig-1 and wrt-6 mutants show enhanced ADL neurosecretion and O2 responses despite being expressed in glia, suggesting indirect effects on ADL sensory perception through glial support of cilia development.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by neurosecretion and behavioral data (Figures 4B, 4C, 4D) and citations to previous work on glial function. The indirect mechanism is inferred from the glial expression pattern and known roles of these genes in cilia development.

results.result: Cross-modal plasticity, where loss of one sensory modality enhances responses to other sensory inputs, is observed across species but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C13, and C113 establish the broader context and motivation for the study. These are supported by citations to previous work in humans and other vertebrates and represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Prior work has established that O2 experience modulates pheromone responses in C. elegans through the URX-RMG hub-and-spoke circuit, with NPR-1 acting in RMG to inhibit circuit output.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 summarize relevant prior work and are supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide essential background for understanding the current study's circuit context.

results.result: BBS genes encode components of the BBSome complex involved in intraflagellar transport, and bbs mutants show sensory defects, increased ADL neurosecretion, and various physiological phenotypes that can be suppressed by gcy-35 mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C52, C103, C105, and C106 summarize relevant prior work on BBS genes and are supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for interpreting the bbs-7 results in the current study.

results.result: The authors speculate that reconfigured peptidergic circuits may be a common feature of cross-modal recruitment across species.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is explicitly labeled as speculation. While the C. elegans data support peptidergic reconfiguration as a mechanism in this system, extrapolation to other species and systems requires additional evidence. This represents an interesting hypothesis for future work.
